title: Scaling Laws and Spectra of Shallow Neural Networks in the Feature Learning Regime
claim: Excess-risk scaling exponents split into distinct regimes with sharp phase boundaries, each tied to a characteristic spectral shape of learned weights.
layout: 1 phase diagram with colored regions, miniature spectra insets, legend of rates at right
description: A single phase diagram with effective sample count n_eff on the x-axis and regularization λ on the y-axis. The plane is split by black and red lines into colored regions labeled Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, V, VIa and VIb: yellow, blue, green, purple, orange and teal. Most regions contain a small sketch of the weight spectrum. These sketches show a bulk, a spike, isolated outlier eigenvalues, or a power-law tail. Red lines mark sharp phase boundaries. A dotted line marks a crossover. Axis ticks and boundary curves carry formulas such as λ = n_eff/d^{1/2}. A legend on the right matches each color to its excess-risk rate R, for example R ≍ d/n_eff. The eye goes first to the colored regions, then to the spectra.
caption: Excess risk rates of Result [ref] as a function of $n$ and $\lambda(n,d)$, with a sketch of the corresponding spectral properties of the learned weights (Result [ref]). \update{Red lines represent sharp phase boundaries with different rates on two sides.}
abstract: Neural scaling laws underlie many of the recent advances in deep learning, yet their theoretical understanding remains largely confined to linear models. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of scaling laws for quadratic and diagonal neural networks in the feature learning regime. Leveraging connections with matrix compressed sensing and LASSO, we derive a detailed phase diagram for the scaling exponents of the excess risk as a function of sample complexity and weight decay. This analysis uncovers crossovers between distinct scaling regimes and plateau behaviors, mirroring phenomena widely reported in the empirical neural scaling literature. Furthermore, we establish a precise link between these regimes and the spectral properties of the trained network weights, which we characterize in detail. As a consequence, we provide a theoretical validation of recent empirical observations connecting the emergence of power-law tails in the weight spectrum with network generalization performance, yielding an interpretation from first principles.
